front: A 10 kg block on a frictionless surface feels 50 N. Acceleration?
why: F=ma calculation; appears every year

front: A 1000 kg car accelerates from 0 to 30 m/s in 6 seconds. What is the average net force?
why: Net force from kinematics then F=ma; standard two-step calculation

front: A 2 m beam has a 100 N weight 0.5 m from the pivot. Torque?
why: Torque tau=rF calculation; tested every year

front: A 5 kg box is pushed across a floor with a coefficient of kinetic friction of 0.3. What is the frictional force? (g = 9.8 $m/s^{2}$)
why: Kinetic friction f=mu*N calculation; appears every year

front: A block just begins to slide on an incline when {{c1::$\tan\theta = \mu_s$}}.
why: tan(theta)=mu_s slip condition; restated by the Q&A card

front: A box is pressed horizontally against a wall hard enough to stay up. Which force supports its weight?
why: Box on wall supported by static friction; secondary conceptual

front: A car's maximum acceleration on level ground is {{c1::$\mu_s g$}}, independent of {{c1::its mass}}.
why: Max acceleration mu_s*g, mass-independent; common friction reasoning

front: A centrifuge separates blood because denser particles require {{c1::more centripetal force}} than the plasma can supply.
why: Centrifuge centripetal reasoning; plausible passage context

front: A coefficient of friction is {{c1::dimensionless}}, so 0.4 is a plausible value but {{c1::0.4 N}} is not.
why: Coefficient dimensionless; useful answer-choice check

front: A crate sits unsecured in a truck bed. What accelerates it, and how hard can the truck accelerate before it slides?
why: Crate in truck restates the mu_s*g maximum-acceleration card

front: A force applied at the pivot produces torque of:
why: Force at pivot gives zero torque; common torque discrete

front: A patient stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating upward at $a$. The scale reads {{c1::$N = m(g + a)$}}.
why: Elevator apparent weight N=m(g+a); tested every year

front: A plot of friction force versus applied force rises along $y = x$, peaks, drops slightly, then flattens. Explain each region.
why: Friction vs applied force graph regions; standard static-to-kinetic reasoning

front: A plot of net force versus acceleration for one object is a line through the origin with slope {{c1::the mass}}.
why: Slope of F vs a plot equals mass; data-figure reading, secondary

front: A rope pulls a sled carrying a child. What force actually accelerates the child?
why: Sled and child: friction accelerates the child; secondary system-isolation puzzle

front: A scale under a patient in an elevator moving upward at constant velocity reads {{c1::$mg$}}.
why: Constant velocity elevator reads true weight; common discrete

front: A sign hangs from two ropes. What happens to the tension as the ropes are pulled closer to horizontal?
why: Rope tension rises as ropes approach horizontal; common tension conceptual

front: A system is in translational equilibrium when:
why: Translational equilibrium sum F=0 with rotational sum tau=0; foundational

front: An object in uniform circular motion has constant speed but {{c1::nonzero acceleration}}.
why: Uniform circular motion has centripetal acceleration v^2/r; tested every year

front: An object lurches forward the instant it breaks free because {{c1::$\mu_k < \mu_s$}}.
why: mu_k < mu_s explains lurch when breaking free; common discrete

front: An orbiting astronaut is apparently weightless. How could you still measure her mass?
why: Measuring mass in orbit via spring period is a thought-experiment aside

front: Apparent weight of a person in a freely falling elevator is {{c1::zero}}.
why: Free-fall apparent weight zero; standard apparent-weight case

front: As an incline gets steeper, the friction force available {{c1::decreases}}.
why: Steeper incline reduces N and available friction; common incline reasoning

front: At constant applied force, a plot of acceleration versus $1/m$ is a straight line whose slope is {{c1::the applied force}}.
why: Linearizing a vs 1/m is graph-reading trivia

front: At what incline angle does a block just begin to slide?
why: Incline slip angle tan(theta)=mu_s; classic derivation asked every year

front: Atwood machine acceleration is {{c1::$a = (m_1 - m_2)g/(m_1 + m_2)$}}.
why: Atwood machine acceleration; common pulley problem

front: Centripetal force is {{c1::not a separate force}}; it is the net inward component of real forces.
why: Centripetal force is net inward real force, not separate; classic FBD point

front: Does zero net force mean an object is at rest?
why: Zero net force means constant velocity, not rest; Newton's first law tested every year

front: Estimate the friction force acting on a 1000 kg car during a 0.5 g emergency stop.
why: Order-of-magnitude braking friction estimate; plausibility check

front: For a rope with significant mass, tension is greatest {{c1::at the end being pulled}}.
why: Tension gradient in a massive rope is off-outline

front: How do mass and weight differ for an astronaut on the Moon?
why: Mass unchanged, weight scales with g on the Moon; common discrete

front: How do you calculate friction force, and how do static and kinetic friction differ?
why: Static vs kinetic friction with f_s <= mu_s N; core friction model

front: In an elevator accelerating downward at $a$, a hanging mass has rope tension {{c1::$m(g - a)$}}.
why: Downward-accelerating elevator tension m(g-a); standard apparent-weight case

front: In limb traction, how is the net therapeutic force found from two angled cables?
why: Traction vector addition; plausible clinical passage step

front: In skin traction the therapeutic force equals {{c1::the hanging weight}}, while the patient's body must supply {{c1::countertraction}}.
why: Pulley redirects tension in skin traction; clinical application

front: In the standard friction model, friction is independent of which two variables?
why: Friction independent of area and speed; secondary model assumption

front: Inertia depends on:
why: Inertia depends on mass; common discrete

front: Inertia is measured by {{c1::mass}} alone, momentum also requires {{c1::velocity}}, and force requires {{c1::acceleration}}.
why: Inertia vs momentum vs force distinctions; restates the inertia card

front: Is acceleration always in the direction of motion?
why: Acceleration follows net force, not motion; common conceptual

front: Joint reaction forces are typically {{c1::several times body weight}} because muscles act on {{c1::short lever arms}}.
why: Joint reaction force magnitudes are biomechanics trivia

front: Mass $m_1$ on a table with friction is pulled by a hanging mass $m_2$. What is the acceleration?
why: Table mass pulled by hanging mass with friction; second-tier system problem

front: Minimum speed to keep contact at the top of a vertical circle is the square root of {{c1::$gr$}}.
why: Minimum speed at top of vertical circle sqrt(gr); common circular-motion problem

front: On a frictionless banked curve the design speed satisfies {{c1::$\tan\theta = v^2/(rg)$}}.
why: Banked curve tan(theta)=v^2/(rg); less common than flat-curve friction case

front: On an incline of angle $\theta$, weight resolves into which two components?
why: Weight components on an incline mg sin/cos; used in every incline problem

front: State Newton's second law and what it says about net force and acceleration.
why: Newton's second law F=ma statement; foundational

front: The normal force does {{c1::zero}} work on a block sliding down an incline.
why: Normal force does zero work on an incline; common work-energy crossover

front: The normal force on a book and the book's weight are {{c1::not a Newton's third-law pair}}.
why: Normal force and weight are not a third-law pair; tested nearly every year

front: The SI unit of force is equivalent to:
why: Newton in SI base units; discrete asked every year

front: Two blocks in contact are pushed across a table by force $F$. How do you find the contact force between them?
why: Two blocks in contact force; second-tier system isolation problem

front: Two ropes at 60 degrees from vertical hold a 20 kg sign. Estimate the tension in each rope.
why: Two-rope tension calculation at 60 degrees; common static-equilibrium item

front: Weight vs. mass?
why: Weight W=mg vs mass; foundational distinction

front: What defines terminal velocity, and what is the acceleration there?
why: Terminal velocity: drag balances weight, zero acceleration; tested every year

front: What external force propels a walking person forward?
why: Static friction propels walking; classic third-law application

front: What features must a Newton's third-law force pair share?
why: Third-law pair properties on different objects; tested every year

front: What is true of tension throughout an ideal massless rope over a frictionless pulley?
why: Ideal rope tension uniform over frictionless pulley; needed in every pulley problem

front: What must be excluded from a correct free-body diagram?
why: What to exclude from a free-body diagram; common FBD conceptual

front: What sets the maximum speed of a car rounding a flat curve of radius $r$?
why: Flat-curve max speed sqrt(mu_s g r); classic circular-motion calculation

front: When does the normal force on a horizontal floor NOT equal $mg$?
why: When normal force differs from mg; common trap

front: Whiplash in a rear-end collision is a demonstration of {{c1::Newton's first law}}.
why: Whiplash as Newton's first law; passage context

front: Why do knee ligaments experience forces several times body weight during a stiff-legged landing?
why: Knee ligament landing forces are biomechanics trivia

front: Why do two blocks of different mass slide down a frictionless incline together?
why: Frictionless incline a=g sin(theta), mass cancels; tested every year

front: Why does a rider feel heaviest at the bottom of a loop?
why: Apparent weight at bottom of loop N=m(g+v^2/r); common circular-motion item

front: Why does an occupant feel pressed back into the seat when a car accelerates?
why: Restates inertia and normal-force reasoning from the seat example

front: Why does pulling a suitcase by a handle angled upward reduce friction?
why: Angled pull reduces normal force and friction; common friction conceptual

front: Why is $f_s = \mu_s N$ wrong as a general statement?
why: f_s <= mu_s N restates the static-vs-kinetic friction card

front: Why is a lawnmower harder to push at a downward angle than to pull at an upward angle?
why: Lawnmower push vs pull restates the angled-pull card
